claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has limited plastic strain capacity.
The limited plasticity of the baseline alloy is associated with Mo-induced electronegativity mismatch.
Replacing Mo with V at a target level described as about 20 at.% will lower the alloy's overall electronegativity difference.
V has an electronegativity closer than Mo to those of Nb, Zr, Ti, and Hf.
V substitution will reduce local electronegativity disparity and make bonding more uniform in the disordered BCC lattice.
More uniform local bonding will lower the Peierls barrier to dislocation glide.
A lower Peierls barrier will facilitate dislocation motion and promote room-temperature plastic deformation.
The proposed V substitution will not significantly undermine lattice-distortion-based solid-solution strengthening.
An optimized V-substituted alloy will retain a room-temperature compressive yield strength near 1700 MPa.
An optimized V-substituted alloy will increase plastic strain capacity by approximately 20–30% relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The beneficial strength–plasticity effect will occur only within an approximately 10–20% V-for-Mo substitution range.
Exceeding the proposed substitution range could cause phase instability.
Exceeding the proposed substitution range could reduce solid-solution strengthening and compromise yield strength.
Arc melting in an inert atmosphere followed by homogenization at approximately 1200 °C for 24 hours is proposed to produce homogeneous test alloys.

contradictions.description: The substitution amount is internally ambiguous. Because the equiatomic alloy contains 20 at.% Mo, replacing 20 at.% of the total alloy would remove all Mo and is not a partial substitution. In contrast, the phrases '10–20% Mo replacement' and the 10%, 15%, and 20% test levels can mean replacement of only 10–20% of the Mo inventory, corresponding to just 2–4 at.% V.
